reference.source: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR
clinicalPearls: The diagnosis requires both multiple motor tics and one or more vocal (phonic) tics, present at some time during the illness, with onset before age 18 and persistence for more than a year
Tics are sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic movements or vocalisations that wax and wane in severity and often shift in type over time
Many patients experience premonitory urges, an uncomfortable sensation relieved by performing the tic, and can suppress tics temporarily at the cost of rising inner tension
Coprolalia, the involuntary utterance of obscenities, is popularly associated with the condition but actually occurs in only a minority of patients
Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, particularly attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder, which often cause more impairment than the tics
Behavioural treatment, especially comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics including habit reversal training, is first-line; medication is reserved for troublesome tics
Pharmacological options for severe tics include agents acting on dopaminergic transmission and certain alpha-adrenergic agents, chosen by symptom burden and comorbidity
Psychoeducation, school liaison, and treating comorbid conditions usually improve function more than suppressing the tics themselves
reference.pathophysiology: Tourette syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder involving dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, with abnormalities in dopaminergic neurotransmission within the basal ganglia thought to underlie the generation of tics. It is highly heritable with a complex polygenic basis, and environmental and possibly immune-mediated factors may modulate expression, while overlapping circuitry accounts for the frequent association with obsessive-compulsive and attentional symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Provisional (transient) tic disorder or persistent motor or vocal tic disorder
Myoclonus, dystonia, or chorea from a neurological cause
Obsessive-compulsive disorder with compulsions resembling tics
additionalInvestigations: Detailed clinical history and observation of tics over time
Screening for comorbid ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, and mood disorders
Standardised tic severity rating scales to monitor course
Neurological examination to exclude other movement disorders
Further neurological workup only if atypical features suggest a secondary cause
redFlags: Abrupt, explosive onset or neurological signs suggesting a secondary or acquired cause
Severe comorbid depression with suicidal ideation
Marked functional deterioration from comorbid ADHD or obsessive-compulsive symptoms
reference.prognosis: Tics typically emerge in childhood, peak in severity in early adolescence, and then decline in many patients, with a substantial proportion experiencing marked improvement or near-resolution by adulthood. Prognosis for overall function depends heavily on comorbid conditions, which often persist and drive impairment, so their recognition and treatment strongly influence outcome.
pitfalls: Focusing on tic suppression while neglecting more impairing comorbid ADHD or obsessive-compulsive disorder
Assuming coprolalia is required for diagnosis when it is uncommon
Overmedicating mild tics that do not warrant pharmacotherapy
Misinterpreting suppressible tics as voluntary or attention-seeking
Missing an atypical presentation that points to a secondary movement disorder
management: Psychoeducation and reassurance about the natural, waxing-and-waning course, with school and family support
Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, including habit reversal training, as first-line treatment
Identify and treat comorbid attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder, which often cause greater impairment than the tics
Reserve medication for troublesome tics, using an alpha-2 agonist such as clonidine or guanfacine, or a dopamine-blocking agent such as aripiprazole or risperidone
Botulinum toxin injection for disabling focal motor or phonic tics
Consider deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-refractory tics in adults
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across psychiatry, neurology, and psychology
